title: The Voice on the Wrong Tape
author: Lantern Original
summaryTr: Bir kasabanın ses arşivi için hazırlanan sergide, son feribot yolculuğuna ait kayıt yerini anlamsız bir sessizliğe bırakır. Ses teknisyeni Nessa, kayıp kaseti ararken bir hatıranın kim tarafından ve hangi amaçla değiştirilebileceğini sorgular.
paragraphs: The first sound on the tape was a chair moving across a wooden floor. After that came a cough, a faint metallic knock, and almost twelve minutes of silence. Nessa removed her headphones and looked through the glass wall of the listening room. In the exhibition hall, a photograph showed Captain Fen standing beside the old river ferry. Beneath it, freshly printed letters promised visitors the sound of the ferry's final journey. They would hear its bell, its engine, and the captain saying goodbye. Instead, Nessa had spent twelve minutes listening to somebody breathe in a quiet room.

She checked the cassette label again. Number twenty-seven: Last ferry morning. It matched the catalogue, the box, and the list of recordings chosen for the exhibition. The tape itself was grey, with a white label and a small brown mark at one corner. Nessa had played it the previous afternoon. Then it had contained exactly what the catalogue promised, followed by an unexpected conversation she had not yet examined closely. Now the sounds of the river were gone. She pressed rewind, keeping her finger clear of the red recording button. Whatever had happened, she would not add another mistake.

The exhibition was due to open on Saturday. It was Thursday morning. Nessa had been hired for three days to prepare digital copies of recordings donated by local residents. The oldest tapes needed careful handling, so she had started by checking the equipment and making a list of damaged cases. Number twenty-seven had been marked as the main attraction. Its owner, Elliot Fen, was paying for much of the exhibition. His grandfather had run the ferry until a road bridge opened thirty years earlier. Elliot wanted visitors to hear a piece of the town's life that photographs could not preserve.

Clara Moss, the exhibition organiser, entered carrying two rolls of posters. Nessa played the beginning of the tape through a speaker. Clara frowned at the scrape of the chair. 'Are you sure you have the right side?' They listened to the other side, which was empty. Clara put the posters down. Her expression changed from irritation to alarm. 'Could the machine have erased it?' Nessa said that was possible only if someone had recorded over it. Simply playing a cassette could not replace river sounds with a quiet room. A person had been involved, even if the result was accidental.

Clara asked whether Nessa had already made a copy. She had not. The recorder's left channel had failed during testing, and she had spent the afternoon replacing a cable. She had played number twenty-seven only long enough to confirm its contents. At five, she had locked the original in the small steel cabinet with the other selected tapes. The cabinet key stayed in a labelled drawer at reception. This was a community archive, not a bank. Staff and volunteers borrowed it whenever they needed an item, signing a sheet that lay beside the drawer.

Four people had entered the building after Nessa left. Clara had worked on captions until seven. Elliot had delivered a model ferry shortly after six. Owen Price, the volunteer who had repaired the archive's cassette machines, had come to collect a tool bag. Salma, the cleaner, had stayed until half past eight. Nessa wrote their names in her notebook. Clara watched her. 'Please do not make this sound like a crime.' Nessa said they first needed to understand whether the wrong cassette had been put in the case. A simple mix-up was still possible, and easier to correct than an erased recording.

She began with the objects rather than the people. The plastic case was the one she remembered, with a crack across its lower corner. Inside lay a folded paper describing the recording. The cassette's label was handwritten in blue ink. Nessa had photographed each tape the day before to document its condition. She opened the photograph on her laptop and enlarged it. Yesterday's cassette had a small triangle cut from the label's left edge. The tape in front of her did not. There was also no brown mark in the photograph. The recording had not changed. The cassette had.

Clara sat down abruptly. 'Then somebody still has the original.' Nessa hoped so. She placed the substitute in a clear envelope and wrote the time on it. Then she searched the cabinet and all the boxes waiting to be catalogued. There were three other grey cassettes, but none had the damaged label shown in her photograph. One contained church music, one a birthday party, and one instructions for a language course. The missing tape had not simply fallen behind another case. By eleven, Nessa knew exactly what she was searching for, but not who had moved it.

Owen arrived with a replacement cable and listened to the news without surprise. He was a thin man in his thirties who usually spoke to machines before greeting people. 'I told you the key should not stay in that drawer,' he said to Clara. She answered that they had never lost anything before. Nessa asked when he had visited the previous evening. He said he arrived around six forty, went into the workshop, collected his tools, and left. He had not borrowed the key. The signing sheet supported him: the final entry was Clara's name at six ten.

When Nessa showed him the substitute cassette, he recognised the brown mark. It was a burn from the end of a hot tool. He had used that cassette to test old recorders because nobody wanted the original contents. The label had said Test three. Now a new label covered it. Owen carefully lifted one loose corner, without removing the whole thing, and showed Nessa the old writing beneath. The substitute had come from the archive's own workshop. That reduced the chance that a visitor had planned the theft in advance. It did not tell them who had taken it.

The workshop contained boxes of cables, a large table, and two recorders. One machine had a cracked battery cover. The other belonged to Owen and had a working microphone. Nessa asked whether he had tested it recently. 'Yesterday afternoon, before you arrived,' he said. 'I recorded the room for a while, then played it back.' He remembered Clara asking him to lower the volume because she was talking on the phone. The chair scrape might therefore be part of his test. The silent tape was not necessarily a recording of the person who replaced the original. Nessa crossed out one tempting idea.

Elliot came at noon in a dark coat, carrying a folder of family photographs. He was angry when Clara explained the problem. At first, he directed his anger towards Nessa, asking why she had not copied the recording immediately. She described the faulty cable and showed him the two cassette photographs. Elliot stopped speaking. He recognised the cut in the original label. His grandfather had done that to distinguish this tape from a similar one. 'The recording belongs to me,' he said. 'If it does not turn up today, I will report it missing.' Nessa told him that was his decision.

Asked about the previous evening, Elliot said he had arrived at six fifteen and stayed for about twenty minutes. Clara had helped him carry the model into the hall. He had looked at the display and left. Had he opened the cabinet? No. Had he listened to the tape before donating it? Not for several years. He remembered the ferry bell and his grandfather speaking. Nessa asked about the conversation after the farewell. Elliot looked puzzled. 'There is only engine noise after that.' She did not correct him yet. Her memory of the voices was brief and uncertain.

Salma was easier to find than Nessa expected. She worked at a nearby bakery during the day and recognised Clara's number when Nessa called. She had seen Elliot leave, then Owen. Clara had remained upstairs for a while before saying goodnight. Salma had cleaned the listening room last because somebody was using it earlier. Nessa asked who. 'I saw a coat through the glass,' Salma said. 'Dark blue or black. I did not look closely.' Both Clara and Elliot had worn dark coats. Salma could not give an exact time, and Nessa made sure not to turn her uncertainty into a fact.

Back in the hall, Nessa examined the listening room. Its glass wall faced the main entrance, but half of it was covered by a hanging exhibition banner. A person at the recorder could be seen only from certain angles. The chair had felt pads underneath its legs. It would not make the harsh scrape heard on the substitute. The workshop chairs had bare wooden feet, confirming Owen's explanation. Beside the recorder lay a stack of blank labels, a blue pen, and a ruler. Anyone preparing the exhibition could have made the false label without bringing materials from outside.

Nessa looked at the writing again. Last ferry morning appeared in neat capital letters, just as it did in the catalogue. The number twenty-seven was written beneath it. There was one small difference: the writer had added an apostrophe to Ferrys in a second line describing the ferry's bell. It was a reasonable correction of the old label's mistake. It suggested someone who cared about presentation even while hiding something. Clara corrected captions for a living. Elliot was a printer. Owen complained about unclear equipment labels. Nessa noted the detail without allowing it to choose a suspect for her.

She asked Clara to show her the exhibition files. The main caption described Captain Fen as the last person to guide the ferry across the river. A longer paragraph praised his devotion to the town. Next to it was a planned listening extract lasting three minutes and forty seconds. Nessa remembered that the voices she had heard began later than that. 'Who chose the end point?' she asked. Clara said Elliot had wanted a short piece for visitors. It ended after the farewell. There was no reason to include several minutes of engine noise. Her explanation sounded sensible, except that Nessa had heard words among those sounds.

At four, Owen returned to collect the broken cable. He glanced at the caption and made an unpleasant sound. 'Still the same story, then.' Nessa asked what he meant. His mother, Lena Price, had worked on the ferry. According to her, Captain Fen had not steered its final crossing. His eyesight had become poor, and Lena had taken the controls while he stood beside the passengers. 'She never got her name on anything,' Owen said. He had asked Clara to change the caption. Clara said a family memory was not enough evidence to contradict the existing records.

Here was a motive that seemed almost too clear. Owen wanted the exhibition to tell a different story. He knew the machines, owned the test cassette, and had entered the building after the original was locked away. If he had removed the main attraction, he could delay the opening or force Clara to change the display. Nessa asked why he had not mentioned the disagreement earlier. 'Because you would look at me exactly as you are doing now.' He folded the cable and put it in his bag. She realised that she had stopped asking questions and started arranging his answers into a familiar shape.

Instead of accusing him, Nessa asked to speak to his mother. Lena lived in a flat overlooking the river and agreed to a visit that evening. She was older than Nessa expected, with strong hands and a quiet way of speaking. On her kitchen wall hung a photograph of the ferry crew. Captain Fen stood at the centre. Lena stood beside the engine cover, half hidden by another man's shoulder. She pointed to herself without bitterness. 'There I am.' She did not claim to have owned the ferry or run its business. She had worked on it for twelve years.

Lena remembered the final morning clearly. A recorder had stood on a box near the front window. Captain Fen had welcomed the passengers and made his speech. Then Lena had taken the ferry across. Near the far bank, he had said something to her about the last rope. Nessa asked for the exact words. Lena shook her head. 'Memory is not a machine. I remember what happened. I cannot give you every sentence.' Nessa liked that answer more than a perfect quotation. Lena had no copy of the tape. She had not known it still existed until Owen mentioned the exhibition.

Nessa asked why Lena had not corrected the story before. She said that at first there had been nothing to correct. Everybody who worked on the ferry knew who had done what. Later, newspaper pieces became shorter and photographs were used without explanation. Captain Fen became the whole ferry. 'He was not a bad man,' she added. 'He paid me fairly. But he liked people looking at him.' Lena did not want the exhibition cancelled. She wanted the work described accurately. If the tape proved she was mistaken, she would accept that too. Nessa left with more questions and a smaller appetite for easy blame.

At home that night, Nessa reviewed the photograph of the original cassette. On the right spool was a narrow strip of red tape, used to attach a repaired section. Owen had told her he had never opened number twenty-seven because it played normally. Elliot remembered his grandfather repairing it after a jam. This meant the cassette could be identified even if somebody removed the label. Nessa sent the image to Clara and asked that nothing from the exhibition be thrown away. Clara replied immediately: Understood. Then a second message arrived asking whether the opening could still happen without the sound.

The question disturbed Nessa. Clara had spent the morning treating the tape as essential. Now she was considering its absence as a practical inconvenience. That might simply be sensible planning under pressure. Nessa knew organisers had to keep working even when something went wrong. Still, she wrote down the change. She also remembered Clara's first question: had Nessa already made a copy? Anyone would ask that, but the answer mattered differently to someone who wanted to recover the recording and someone who wanted certain words to disappear. The same sentence could point in opposite directions.

On Friday morning, Nessa asked each person to describe their evening again, without suggesting that earlier answers were wrong. Elliot repeated his times and produced a parking receipt ending at six thirty-eight. It did not prove every minute, but it supported his account of leaving early. Owen showed a message he had sent his partner from the bus stop at six fifty-two. Salma remembered that Clara said goodnight just after the radio news began in the kitchen. The news started at seven. Nessa now had a likely sequence, though she kept the word likely in front of it.

Clara said she had spent the period after Elliot left changing captions upstairs. She had used the cabinet key earlier to check a photograph number, which explained her signature at six ten. Nessa asked whether she had entered the listening room. 'Briefly. I wanted to hear whether the new speaker worked.' Which cassette had she played? Clara answered, 'The ferry tape, obviously.' It was the first time she had admitted listening to it that evening. When Nessa asked why she had not mentioned this before, Clara said nobody had asked specifically. That was true, but it was not reassuring.

According to Clara, the recording had sounded normal. She had stopped it after the captain's farewell, returned it to its case, and locked the cabinet. Nessa asked whether she had noticed a chair scrape at the start. Clara said no. If that account was accurate, the substitution had happened later. Only Owen and Salma were known to remain after Elliot left, and Clara herself stayed until seven. Nessa could not eliminate anybody on timing alone. She thanked Clara and went to the workshop, where she played Owen's other test cassettes. Each began with him speaking the date and naming the machine.

The substitute did not contain that spoken introduction. Its quiet room recording began abruptly with the chair moving. Owen listened and remembered that on Wednesday he had stopped the test, moved the cassette forward, and recorded again. The first part still ought to be on the tape. Nessa checked the tape counter and rewound completely. A few seconds before the scrape, at very low volume, was Owen saying, 'Second test, after lunch.' She had missed it because the machine had not been fully rewound when she first played it. The discovery settled one question and created another.

The false label could not have been on the test cassette while Owen was using it, because he remembered reading Test three. Therefore the substitution happened after his afternoon work. More importantly, the cassette had been left partly played, close to the chair scrape. Someone checking only its opening might believe it was blank. Nessa wondered whether the person who replaced the original had chosen the test cassette because it looked empty, without listening to all of it. That would fit a hurried decision better than a carefully prepared theft. She began looking for evidence of what had changed during Wednesday evening.

She found it in a wastepaper box under the caption desk. Clara had asked everyone to separate clean paper for reuse, so old drafts remained stacked rather than torn up. One draft of the ferry caption included a sentence absent from the final version: The last crossing was completed by the crew under Captain Fen's direction. Another named Lena Price as a crew member. A third returned to the claim that the captain himself guided the ferry across. Nessa arranged them by the printed times at the bottom. All three had been produced between six forty and six fifty-eight on Wednesday.

The drafts did not prove theft. They did prove that Clara had been reconsidering the story that evening. Nessa took them upstairs. Clara looked at the pages and sighed. Owen's complaint had made her try different versions, she said. She had rejected them because there was still no proof. Nessa asked why the most general version required more proof than the specific claim about Captain Fen steering. Clara answered that the existing caption had already been approved by Elliot. For the first time, she sounded defensive about the exhibition rather than the missing object.

Nessa asked to see the email approving the caption. Clara opened the shared project mailbox. Elliot's message contained several corrections, but also a clear sentence: If the archive finds an error, please let me know before printing. He had not demanded that his grandfather be described as the person at the controls. Clara had inferred that changing the story might upset the sponsor. When Nessa pointed this out, Clara said the situation was more complicated than one email. The building needed funding for its winter programme. Elliot had offered to help. Nessa could see the pressure, but pressure was not evidence of what he would actually do.

Downstairs, Salma arrived with the bakery's spare cardboard boxes. She saw Nessa examining the listening room and said she had remembered another detail. The person inside had been holding a white card close to the glass, perhaps reading it in the light. It had looked like a postcard from a distance. Nessa asked whether it might have been a cassette label. Salma said she could not tell. Nessa did not press her. Beside the recorder, however, the stack of blank labels had a missing corner where one label had been peeled away. That was ordinary enough in a busy archive, but the white card now had a possible purpose.

The decisive clue came from the model ferry. Elliot wanted to take it home if the exhibition could not open as promised. Nessa helped lift its clear cover and noticed a paper envelope beneath the wooden base. It contained the model's instructions, a small screwdriver, and a dark blue receipt. Elliot recognised the receipt. Clara had placed it there when he delivered the model, to keep it from getting lost. It was for a storage box she had bought that afternoon. The shop's product description said Four cassette cases, clear. Nessa looked at the new cases stacked beside the display.

Three cases were empty. The fourth was missing. This did not show where the original cassette had gone, but it suggested it might have been moved into a new case rather than carried loose. Nessa asked Clara about it. Clara said the fourth case had been cracked and thrown away. Nessa remembered her instruction that nothing should be discarded. Clara said she had thrown it out before receiving that message. Owen, who had unpacked the cases for her on Wednesday, quietly said they had all been sound. Clara answered too quickly that he must have missed the crack.

Nessa did not search Clara's bag or coat. Instead, she asked everyone to stop moving exhibition material until they had checked the remaining archive boxes together. Elliot agreed and said he would make the missing-property report after lunch if the tape was still absent. Clara looked towards the stairs. On the upper landing stood several boxes marked Winter programme. They contained display material that would not be opened for months. Nessa asked whether the spare cassette case could have been packed by mistake. Clara said she would check them herself. Nessa answered that it would be quicker if they all helped.

Clara remained still. Then she said, 'It is in the box with the school photographs.' Nobody spoke for a moment. Nessa asked what was in the box. 'The tape.' Clara sat on the bottom stair as if her legs had suddenly weakened. Elliot went upstairs, but Nessa asked him to wait while she fetched the box with him. Inside, between two folders of photographs, was a clear cassette case. The grey tape had a triangular cut in its label. Through the window above the right spool, Nessa could see the narrow red repair strip. It was number twenty-seven.

They played it together. The ferry bell rang, followed by the low engine and passengers talking. Captain Fen welcomed everyone and thanked the town for supporting his family. He spoke slowly, enjoying the occasion. After his farewell, footsteps crossed the deck. Then his voice came again, quieter now. 'Lena, take her over. I cannot see the far marker clearly today.' A woman answered, 'I have it.' The engine changed its note. Several minutes later, the captain thanked Lena for the smooth crossing and asked her to bring the final rope. Nothing in the conversation sounded secret or shameful.

Clara had heard those words on Wednesday. She admitted that she had played farther than the chosen extract because she wanted to check for useful background sound. The conversation contradicted the central caption. Elliot had just spoken enthusiastically about extending his support to other projects. Clara imagined him seeing the correction as an attack on his grandfather. She tried different captions, disliked each one, and decided to remove the tape until after the opening. The test cassette had offered a way to make the loss look like an old recording that had failed. She had assumed its quiet contents were blank.

'I was going to find it later,' she said. Elliot looked at her for a long time. 'And tell me what? That my grandfather's voice had come back?' Clara covered her face with her hands. Nessa asked why she had not simply explained the recording. Clara said she had been afraid of losing the funding, the winter programme, and her own position. Once she had made the substitution, every question had required another answer that was not quite true. Hiding the original among future displays had bought time. It had also made an honest return increasingly difficult.

Elliot did not offer immediate forgiveness. He said his donation had included an agreement that the original would be protected and returned after copying. Clara had broken that trust. He wanted a written account of what had happened and a meeting with the archive committee before deciding about further support. He would postpone reporting the cassette as missing because it was now recovered, but he would not pretend there had been an innocent mix-up. Nessa placed the original in a new envelope and wrote a receipt when she returned it to him after making two checked digital copies.

Owen stood beside the window, looking less satisfied than Nessa expected. He said he should have insisted that they interview his mother before printing anything. Clara apologised for dismissing Lena's account and for allowing suspicion to fall on him. He accepted that she had spoken but did not say everything was settled. Nessa thought this was fair. Recovering an object could happen in minutes. Repairing what people had said and assumed might take much longer. She also apologised to Owen for treating his anger as evidence. He nodded. 'It was a reason to ask,' he said. 'Not a reason to decide.'

They telephoned Lena and played the relevant section with Elliot's permission. She listened without interrupting. After the captain's thanks, she gave a small laugh. 'He always asked for that rope before we were properly stopped.' Elliot asked whether she would come to the exhibition and help correct the crew information. Lena said she would, provided nobody turned her into the only person who had done any work. There had been four people keeping the ferry running on the final day. She could name them all. Elliot found a pencil and began writing, asking her to spell one surname twice.

The opening moved from Saturday morning to Saturday afternoon. A short notice explained that the archive was correcting information and replacing a damaged display panel. It did not invent an equipment failure. Clara stepped back from handling original recordings while the committee reviewed the incident. Nessa set up a simple borrowing record with a named person responsible for each item. The cabinet key moved out of the public drawer. These changes would not make dishonesty impossible, but they would make objects easier to trace and uncertain memories less important. The archive could remain welcoming without treating every precaution as an insult.

On Saturday, the new caption described the final crossing as the work of a crew. Captain Fen still stood at the centre of the photograph, because that was where he had stood when it was taken. Beside it was a second photograph Lena had brought from home, showing the engine room with two workers inside. The listening extract continued beyond the captain's speech. Visitors could hear him asking for help, Lena answering, and the ferry reaching the bank. The longer recording did not make him smaller. It gave the scene more people and made the work easier to understand.

Nessa watched a child press the play button while his father read the caption. When the engine changed its sound, the child asked who was driving. His father pointed to Lena's name. A few steps away, Lena and Elliot were discussing a face in another photograph. Clara stood at the welcome desk, answering questions quietly. There would be a committee meeting on Monday and difficult decisions after it. For now, the original cassette was back with its owner, the copies had been checked, and the story on the wall matched the voices. Nessa closed her notebook and listened to the ferry arrive.

phrases.tr: suç gibi görünmek, suç izlenimi vermek

quiz.q: What first proves that the original cassette was replaced rather than erased?
options: A difference in the printed exhibition dates
The damaged label visible in Nessa's earlier photograph
A message from Lena
The missing cabinet key
quiz.explainTr: Önceki fotoğraftaki etiketin üçgen kesik köşesi yeni kasette yoktur; fiziksel kaset değiştirilmiştir.

quiz.q: Why is the quiet recording not reliable evidence of who made the substitution?
options: It was recorded by Owen during an earlier equipment test
It contains several clearly identified voices
Nessa accidentally recorded it herself
It was made thirty years earlier on the ferry
quiz.explainTr: Odadaki sessiz kayıt, Owen'ın daha önce yaptığı cihaz testine aittir; kaseti değiştiren kişinin ses kaydı değildir.

quiz.q: What assumption leads Clara to hide the original?
options: Lena wants the whole exhibition cancelled
Owen intends to sell the cassette
Correcting the captain's role will make Elliot withdraw his support
The original is too damaged to play safely
quiz.explainTr: Clara, açıklamanın düzeltilmesinin bağışçıyı kızdırıp desteği kaybettireceğini varsayar; bunu Elliot'a sormaz.

quiz.q: What does the recovered recording establish?
options: Captain Fen never worked on the ferry
The final journey was cancelled
Elliot changed the recording himself
Lena operated the ferry during its final crossing
quiz.explainTr: Kaptan karşı kıyıdaki işareti net göremediği için Lena'dan feribotu kullanmasını ister ve sonra ona teşekkür eder.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes the ending?
options: The recording is recovered and corrected, while the breach of trust still needs review
All characters immediately forgive Clara
The exhibition removes every mention of Captain Fen
Nessa keeps the original cassette as evidence forever
quiz.explainTr: Kayıt sahibine döner ve sergi düzeltilir; ancak Clara'nın güveni zedeleyen davranışı kurul tarafından ayrıca ele alınacaktır.
